lesson.title: Sharing the Container: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
lesson.summary: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a mixture of gases equals the sum of the pressures each individual gas would exert if it alone occupied the whole container.
lesson.body:
Everything so far has treated gas pressure as coming from a single kind of particle, but most real gas samples, air being the obvious example, are mixtures. Dalton's law addresses exactly this situation: it says that each gas in a mixture contributes its own share of the total pressure, called its partial pressure, completely independently of the other gases present, and the total pressure is simply the sum of all the partial pressures. In symbols, P_total = P1 + P2 + P3 and so on for as many gases as are present.

This follows directly from the ideal gas model and connects back to gas pressure as a collision-frequency phenomenon. Because ideal gas particles do not interact with each other except during brief, elastic collisions, each type of gas molecule bombards the container walls exactly as often as it would if it were alone in that same volume at that same temperature. The nitrogen molecules in air do not know or care that oxygen molecules are also present; they just keep colliding with the walls at a rate set by their own concentration and speed. Add up the collision contributions from every gas present, and you get the total pressure.

A worked example shows that this is not just a rule to memorize but something you can verify directly from PV = nRT. Suppose a 5.00 L container at 300 K holds 0.10 mol of nitrogen gas and 0.20 mol of oxygen gas. Calculate the partial pressure of each gas separately using PV = nRT, rearranged to P = nRT/V. For nitrogen: P(N2) = (0.10 mol)(0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K) / (5.00 L). The numerator is 0.10 times 0.0821 times 300, which is 2.463, and dividing by 5.00 gives 0.493 atm. For oxygen: P(O2) = (0.20)(0.0821)(300) / 5.00. The numerator is 4.926, and dividing by 5.00 gives 0.985 atm. Adding the two partial pressures: 0.493 + 0.985 = 1.478 atm, so the total pressure should be about 1.48 atm.

You can check this answer a completely different way, which is exactly the kind of consistency check worth doing on any gas law problem. Instead of calculating each gas separately, just add the moles first: 0.10 mol + 0.20 mol = 0.30 mol total, then plug that directly into PV = nRT: P_total = (0.30)(0.0821)(300) / 5.00 = 7.389 / 5.00 = 1.48 atm. Both methods agree, which is exactly what Dalton's law guarantees: it does not matter whether you treat the mixture as one combined sample or as separate gases added together, the total pressure comes out the same either way.
